clue.text: Illustrate key opening prison after revolution with touch of euphoria

indicators.note: the key goes in and opens up the turned-round prison word, sitting inside it
a revolution turns the prison word round so it is read backwards

parts.note: bird is slang for a prison sentence, and by extension prison
Esc is the escape key on a keyboard

indicators.note: just a touch of the word euphoria, its first letter

explanation.surface: An artist tries to depict a key unlocking a jail after an uprising, with a hint of joy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after revolution' gives DRIB. Bird is British slang for prison time, from rhyming slang 'bird lime' for time.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to illustrate something is to depict or portray it in words or pictures.

clue.text: Obligation to lift bottom onto end of seat

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting a word makes it read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a bed is the bottom of a river or the sea

indicators.note: the end of seat is its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone is told they must raise their backside on to the edge of a chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottom' suggests a backside, but it is the seabed or river bed; 'to lift' gives DEB in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an obligation to pay money owed is a liability of that kind.

clue.text: Sound of the seaside? Yes!

indicators.note: the clue asks for what a word sounds like when spoken

parts.note: the seaside is the shore

explanation.surface: Asked whether they heard the waves at the beach, someone answers with an enthusiastic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent SHORE and SURE can sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Exclamation: saying it means agreeing emphatically, just like an eager affirmative.

clue.text: Singer breaking rules

indicators.note: breaking the word singer apart lets its letters be rearranged

explanation.surface: A vocalist defies the regulations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rules' looks like a plural noun but is a verb: a monarch rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a monarch who rules a country holds the throne and governs it.

clue.text: Large ship, huge fighter transporting stock, heading for the bottom

indicators.note: the fighter carries the livestock word inside him

parts.note: a bruiser is a big, tough fighter

indicators.note: the first letter of the livestock word goes to its end, the bottom of a down entry

parts.note: cattle are livestock, often called stock

explanation.surface: A hulking boxer ferries livestock to the seabed aboard a big vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading for the bottom' gives ATTLEC; 'the bottom' sounds like sinking but means the foot of this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a battlecruiser is a big warship, heavily armed like a battleship but faster.

clue.text: Destroy vessel, carve into it

indicators.note: the carving word goes into the vessel word

parts.note: a cup is a drinking vessel
to hew is to carve or chop

explanation.surface: A vandal wrecks a pot by gouging into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Phrasal verb: to destroy something by mangling it, as a machine mangles a tape.

clue.text: Introduction to a Persian poet not right — it's cheese

parts.note: hallo, a greeting, is how one introduces oneself

indicators.note: the letter standing for right is removed

parts.note: Rumi was a thirteenth-century Persian poet
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A greeting to a Persian poet who is not quite right turns out to be about cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to a' are link words, giving the surface its sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: halloumi is a firm salty cheese from Cyprus, often grilled.

clue.text: Someone enjoying alcohol, one not saving water in Newcastle, says Spooner?

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words trade places

parts.note: the Tyne is the river that runs through Newcastle
a waster squanders rather than saves

explanation.surface: A drinker, described by the famously muddled Spooner, as someone who squanders Newcastle's water.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of TYNE WASTER gives WINE TASTER; Spooner was an Oxford don known for such slips.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a professional or amateur who samples vintages appreciates drink.

clue.text: Good cord that binds on engine component

parts.note: pi, short for pious, means good

indicators.note: the cord wraps round and so binds the word on

parts.note: a string is a cord

explanation.surface: A sturdy rope that ties things to a motor part.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a piston ring seals the gap between a piston and its cylinder in an engine.

clue.text: Brief title recalled in trade

indicators.note: the turned-round title goes in the trade word

parts.note: to barter is to trade

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the title word is read backwards

parts.note: Sir is a title

explanation.surface: A short heading is remembered in commerce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective but is the noun: British slang for a lawyer.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: a brief is a lawyer, one who takes the brief for a case in court.

clue.text: Almost everything in book and novel runs an old dated system?

indicators.note: the shortened everything word goes in the book word

parts.note: a romance is a book, a love story

indicators.note: almost all of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: all means everything
the final letter removed

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are given a new order

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Nearly everything in a book and a novel uses an antiquated system of dating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges AND into NDA. 'novel' also tempts as a synonym for book; here it is the shuffle signal, and the book is a romance.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: the Romans' calendar reckoned dates by kalends, nones and ides, a long-obsolete system.

clue.text: Reported feline relationships

indicators.note: reported means spoken of, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a lynx is a wild feline

explanation.surface: Word has it that the cat has connections.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: links between people or things are ties or connections.

clue.text: Choice of camels, husband exchanged for fifty — how sweet?

indicators.note: the husband letter is swapped out and the fifty letter takes its place

parts.note: a camel has one hump (dromedary) or two (Bactrian)
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A camel buyer swaps a husband for fifty, while someone asks about sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the host's question about sugar lumps in tea asks how sweetened the guest wants it.

clue.text: Held by communists after uprising, veteran prisoner getting ground cleaner

indicators.note: the veteran and prisoner are held inside the communists word
in a down entry an uprising reads the communists word upwards

parts.note: reds are communists
OAP, old-age pensioner, is a veteran
POW is a prisoner of war

explanation.surface: An old prisoner of war captured by rebelling communists is given a grinding cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after uprising' gives SDER in this down entry. 'ground' reads as a verb but describes the powder's milled form.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: washing powder is a detergent milled into fine granules, hence ground.

clue.text: Told you so! Cameron always PM!

parts.note: there! is said when proved right
Sam, Samantha Cameron, wife of former PM David Cameron
ay is an old word for always

explanation.surface: A gloating cry that David Cameron should have been prime minister for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests David Cameron, but it is his wife's name that is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: she was the British Prime Minister who followed David Cameron in 2016.

clue.text: I see you on old Hawaiian island

indicators.note: in an across answer, one piece placed on another comes after it, so old goes first

parts.note: ah is said on understanding something
U is text shorthand for you

explanation.surface: Someone recognises a friend on an ancient Pacific island.
explanation.definitionFit: Geography: it is the Pacific island in the Hawaii chain home to Honolulu.

clue.text: Green no Scrooge, a saver

parts.note: eco- means environmentally friendly, green
Scrooge, from Dickens, is a byword for a miser

explanation.surface: An environmentalist, no skinflint, is nonetheless a thrifty person.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: someone or something that cuts consumption is a thrifty device or person.

clue.text: Daily Mail ultimately so shabby, not to be trusted?

indicators.note: shabby means scruffy and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: Daily and so are taken as written, and Mail ultimately gives only its final letter, L, between them

explanation.surface: A dig at the Daily Mail newspaper as tatty and untrustworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mail is a British tabloid. 'ultimately' takes just the last letter of Mail; 'shabby' then jumbles that with DAILY and SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: someone faithless or treacherous cannot be relied upon.

clue.text: Certain fact

definitions.meaning: certain as in a specific one, this certain person
a fact or detail, as in giving the details of something

explanation.surface: A definite truth.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: an adjective meaning specific, and a noun meaning an individual detail.

clue.text: Youth getting through cigarette ends

indicators.note: the answer runs through the words, across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A young person is smoking cigarettes down to the stubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a youth is a young person, an adolescent between thirteen and nineteen.

clue.text: Two groups without leadership getting flak

indicators.note: two of the groups, so the word is written twice
without its leading letter, the first one

parts.note: a pack is a group
the leading letter removed

explanation.surface: Two leaderless factions get criticised.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: ack-ack is anti-aircraft fire, from old signallers' alphabet, which is flak.

clue.text: Celebs so unrecognisable in previously outmoded state

indicators.note: the jumbled celebrities go inside the previously word

parts.note: once means previously

indicators.note: something unrecognisable has been changed beyond knowing, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Former celebrities have faded so far they cannot be recognised, their fame long out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unrecognisable' gives BSOLESCE, split around by the word for previously.
explanation.definitionFit: Noun sense: the state of being out of date or no longer useful.

clue.text: Filth seems moderate under Tories for starters

indicators.note: starters means the first letters of the words

explanation.surface: Smut seems to be reined in under a Conservative government.
explanation.walkthrough: Tories are the UK Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: smut is filth, obscene or indecent material.

clue.text: Girl who may turn up?

definitions.note: the girl's name is the same read upwards as downwards

indicators.note: in a down entry turning up means reading upwards, and the name is unchanged that way

parts.note: the girl's name is the same read upwards as downwards

explanation.surface: A girl who might drop by unannounced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn up' suggests arriving; it means the name reads the same upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Anna is a girl's name.

clue.text: Idiot, a blend of parents?

definitions.meaning: the start of daddy fused with the end of mummy, a portmanteau of the two parent words

explanation.surface: A child is called a fool and a mix of mother and father.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: slang for a fool, and a playful blend of dad and mum's names.

clue.text: Fish me, dorsal fin at the back, swimming

indicators.note: swimming letters move about freely, so they are rearranged
the back of fin is its last letter

explanation.surface: A fish talks about its own dorsal fin as it swims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swimming' rearranges ME DORSAL into REDSALMO; the fin's back letter then closes the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: red salmon, or sockeye, is a Pacific salmon with deep red flesh.

clue.text: Eliminate gold counters, as sovereigns

indicators.note: counters means goes against, so the words are run in the opposite direction

parts.note: to slay is to eliminate, to kill
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Someone disposes of gold tokens, playing at being kings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'counters' looks like a noun, gaming pieces, but is a verb signalling reversal of SLAYOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: sovereigns are kings and queens, members of the royal family.

clue.text: A blast from the past, one pulled by puller, we hear?

indicators.note: the clue says the phrase is heard spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a cracker is pulled at Christmas, and the one pulling it, towing it, is a tower

explanation.surface: A nostalgic phrase for something old, riddled with pulling.
explanation.walkthrough: A Christmas cracker is a paper tube pulled apart with a bang; said in a British accent, cracker tower approximates the volcano.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the volcano's 1883 eruption was one of history's most violent explosions.
